fact_sheet.business_description: the Company is a West Coast producer and retailer of boxed chocolates with a strong California reputation [D01]. It operates more than 150 shops and offers more than 60 candy varieties [D03].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Boxed chocolates sold for personal consumption and as gifts; customer loyalty is driven by dependable quality and an established local name [D01, D03, D06].
economics: Pretax earnings margin of approximately 13–14.5% [D02, D06].
Implied after-tax return on tangible capital of approximately 25–29% [D02].
Profits depend on realized price per pound after accounting for ingredients, labor, occupancy, and selling costs [D01, D06].
competitive_position: Moat evidence rests on durable customer relationships and brand recognition, though subject to potential substitution by other sweets or gifts [D01, D03, D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Net tangible operating capital: approximately $7–8m [D02, D03].
Requires inventory, staffing, and maintenance of product freshness [D01, D06].
management_and_capital_allocation: Operating manager is to be evaluated for continuity [D01].
Management record is part of the overall assessment, but specific details are not in pack [D01].

yields_pct.basis: Earnings yield calculated as approximately $2m net income divided by $25m price [D04]; long bond yield is 10-year Treasury rate as of Jan 3, 1972 [D04].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Regional name may not justify premium over tangible assets [D05].
Ingredient, wage, and occupancy cost inflation may absorb price increases [D05].
Risks associated with expansion outside California [D05].
recent_events: Not in pack (beyond historical fiscal summaries ending in 1971) [D02, D03].
berkshire_context: Buyer is the Company, a vehicle associated with Buffett and Munger [D08].
document_conflicts: Sales figure for FY1971 is stated as 'just over $28m' [D02, D03] while general 'entry-scale annual' revenue is cited as '$29–30m' [D02, D03].
missing_data: Full balance sheet, complete debt/cash positions, exact FY1971 earnings, and detailed historical capex/depreciation/FCF figures [D02, D04].

understandable.evidence: The company operates a simple, long-established business model of producing and retailing boxed chocolates [D01, D03].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: Customer loyalty is driven by dependable quality and a strong established regional brand in California [D01, D03, D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: The business demonstrates consistent profitability with annual pretax earnings of approximately $4–4.2m on sales of $29–30m [D02, D03].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The business generates an after-tax return on tangible capital of approximately 25–29% [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The business requires only $7–8m in net tangible operating capital to generate substantial annual earnings [D02, D03].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Specific management details are not in the pack, and the manager is yet to be evaluated for continuity [D01].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: At a $25m valuation, this acquisition is appropriate for the current era's investment goals [D04].

price_screen.evidence: The pretax earnings yield of ~16% (based on $4m earnings vs $25m price) is well above the 1.5x long bond yield threshold of 8.91% [D04].

conflicts_resolved: The sales figure conflict ($28m vs $29-30m) was resolved by using the consistent $29-30m entry-scale figure for evaluating the scale of operations [D02, D03].
gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a branded regional producer with strong returns on tangible capital and a defensible local franchise

gate2.why_available: The market likely views this as a localized, capital-intensive retail operation subject to inflationary pressures on labor and ingredients, leading to a modest valuation [D05]. We disagree, as the business possesses a durable regional brand moat and generates consistent, high returns on tangible capital that exceed the cost of inflation [D02, D03, D06]. The value will be realized through steady compounding of owner earnings at a price that offers a significant margin of safety [D04].
evidence: Annual pretax earnings of $4–4.2m on a $25m purchase price [D02, D04].
After-tax return on tangible capital of approximately 25–29% [D02].
Established reputation and over 150 shops creating a defensible local franchise [D01, D03].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market worries that the regional name is insufficient to justify a premium over tangible assets and that rising costs for ingredients, labor, and occupancy will erode margins [D05].
what_must_be_true: The regional brand remains durable against substitute sweets or gifts [D01, D06].
Management can maintain pricing power to offset inflationary pressures on operating costs [D05, D06].
The business can continue to operate with minimal incremental capital requirements [D02].

gate3.price_vs_value: Price is ~55-70% of low-end value; significant margin of safety
gate3.alternatives: Long bonds at 5.94% [D04]; we prefer the business as it offers a superior yield and growth potential through a defensible local franchise [D02, D03]
gate3.downside_case: Permanent loss unlikely given tangible asset backing; risk is management inability to pass on costs [D05]
flagged_assumptions: Assumed maintenance capex is negligible relative to $4.1m pretax earnings [D02]
Assumed earnings stability in face of regional inflation [D05]

gate4.role_description: We prefer to purchase 80-100% of a business, leaving existing management to operate the enterprise while we focus on the efficient allocation of the generated cash flows [D04].
value_realisation_path: The value is realized through the steady compounding of owner earnings, which we expect to redeploy into further productive assets [D02, D04].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In the early 1970s, our strategy involves acquiring controlled interests in profitable businesses with minimal capital requirements to serve as cash-generative engines for the partnership's continued growth [D02, D04].

kill_criteria: Inflationary pressure on labor, sugar, and cocoa costs exceeds our ability to raise retail prices
The regional brand loses its consumer loyalty to national competitors or generic substitutes
Management fails to maintain the shop-level standards necessary to protect the brand's reputation
Excessive expansion outside the core California market destroys the economics of the retail footprint
gate5.berkshire_constraints: We must ensure that the $25m cash outlay does not compromise the liquidity needed for our existing trading-stamp obligations [D08].
gate5.opportunity_cost: The capital could otherwise be deployed into marketable securities yielding 8–10% or long bonds at 5.94%, but this acquisition offers superior long-term compounding and a higher initial pretax yield of 16.5% [D04].
gate5.decider_reason: As a whole-business acquisition in the early 1970s, this falls directly under my responsibility to identify cash-generative engines for the partnership [D04].
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is that persistent regional cost inflation outpaces our pricing power, eroding the high returns on tangible capital.

valuation.downside_case: Permanent loss is unlikely given the support of $7-8m in tangible assets; the risk remains that inflationary pressures outpace the ability to raise prices.

drivers.driver: The whole company sells for $25m, representing a pretax earnings yield of 16.5% against a long bond yield of 5.94% [D04].
The business possesses a durable regional brand moat and pricing power in California, evidenced by high customer loyalty [D01, D06].
The company generates consistent annual pretax earnings of $4m on sales of $29-30m with high returns on tangible capital [D02, D03].
The enterprise requires minimal capital investment of only $7-8m, leaving excess cash available for deployment [D02, D03].

kill_criteria: Inflationary pressure on labor, sugar, and cocoa costs exceeds our ability to raise retail prices
The regional brand loses its consumer loyalty to national competitors or generic substitutes
Management fails to maintain the shop-level standards necessary to protect the brand's reputation
final.what_would_change_our_mind: We would reconsider our position if the durability of the brand were to falter or if regional inflation rendered the cost of ingredients and labor permanently incompatible with the price points our customers are willing to accept [D05, D06].
final.memo:
See's Candies is a quintessential consumer franchise, operating a simple and long-established business producing high-quality boxed chocolates [D01, D03]. We understand this business perfectly; it relies on dependable quality and a loyal customer base across more than 150 shops in California, creating a clear and defensible local brand identity [D01, D03, D06].

The economics are exceptional, characterized by an after-tax return on tangible capital of 25–29% [D02]. With annual pretax earnings of approximately $4m on sales of $29–30m, the business requires only $7–8m in net tangible operating capital, providing a highly cash-generative engine for the partnership [D02, D03].

We intend to leave existing management in place to focus on the day-to-day operations while we oversee the allocation of the substantial cash flows generated [D04]. We trust the existing team to maintain the high standards that define the See's reputation [D01].

The market appears to view this as a localized, capital-intensive operation vulnerable to cost inflation [D05]. We believe this perspective ignores the strength of the brand and the pricing power that permits the business to pass cost increases to its customers [D05, D06].

At a $25m purchase price, we are paying roughly 6 times pretax earnings, an initial yield of 16.5% compared to 5.94% available in long-term bonds [D04]. We value this enterprise between $35m and $45m, providing a significant margin of safety [D04].

Like a well-liked local newspaper, the primary risk is that our pricing power fails to keep pace with the costs of ingredients and labor [D05]. We are prepared to hold this business indefinitely, as its reliable returns represent an excellent use of our capital [D04].
